fidelity.e: From Late Middle English fidelite (“allegiance, fealty; faithfulness, trust; agreement made in good faith”), from Old French fidélité (“faithfulness, fidelity”) (modern French fidélité), from Latin fidēlitās (“faithfulness, fidelity”), from fidēlis (“dependable, trustworthy.
fidelity.g: Often followed by to or towards: faithfulness or loyalty towards a person, a group, one's civic or moral duties, etc.; allegiance; (countabl

field.e: From Middle English feld, feeld (“field”), from Old English feld (“field”), from Proto-West Germanic *felþu (“field”), from Proto-Germanic *felþuz (“field”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“field, plain”) or *pleth₂- (“flat”) (with schwebeablaut).
field.g: A land area free of woodland, cities, and towns; an area of open country.

fierce.e: From Middle English fers, fiers, borrowed from Old French fers (“wild", "ferocious”), nominative of fer, from Latin ferus (“wild", "untamed”).
fierce.g: Exceedingly violent, severe, ferocious, cruel or savage.

fiercely.e: From Middle English fersly; equivalent to fierce + -ly.

fierceness.e: From Middle English fersnesse; equivalent to fierce + -ness.

fiery.e: From Middle English fyry, from fyr (“fire”), equivalent to fire + -y.

fifteen.e: From Middle English fiftene, from Old English fīftīene, fīftēne, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun. Equivalent to five + -teen.
fifteen.g: The cardinal number occurring after fourteen (14) and before sixteen (16).

fifteenth.e: From Middle English fiftenthe, fiftethe, from Old English fīftēoþa, equivalent to fifteen + -th.
fifteenth.g: The ordinal form of the number fifteen.

fifth.e: From Middle English fifthe, fifte, fift, from Old English fīfta (“fifth”), from Proto-Germanic *fimftô (“fifth”) or *femftô, equivalent to five + -th (ordinal suffix).
fifth.g: The ordinal form of the number five.

fiftieth.e: From earlier fifteth, from Middle English fiftithe, fyftith; equivalent to fifty + -eth. For the modern form, see the etymological notes at twentieth.
fiftieth.g: The ordinal form of the number fifty.

fifty.e: From Middle English fifty, from Old English fīftiġ, from Proto-Germanic *fimf tigiwiz (“five tens”). By surface analysis, five + -ty.
fifty.g: The cardinal number occurring after forty-nine and before fifty-one.

fig.e: From Middle English fige, fygge (also fyke, from Old English fīc, see fike), borrowed from Anglo-Norman figue, borrowed from Old French figue, from Old Occitan figa, from Vulgar Latin *fīca (“fig”), from Latin fīcus (“fig tree”).
fig.g: The fruit of the fig tree, pear-shaped and containing many small seeds.
To move suddenly or quickly; rove about.

fight.e: From Middle English fighten (“to fight”), from Old English feohtan (“to fight, combat, strive”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to comb, tease, shear, struggle with”), from Proto-Indo-European *peḱ- (“to comb, shear”). Related also to Old English feht (“wool, shaggy pelt, fleece”).

From Middle English fight, feyght, fiȝt, fecht, from Old English feoht, ġefeoht (“fight”), from Proto-West Germanic *fehtan (“to fight”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtą, *gafehtą (“fight, struggle”), from Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to struggle with”).

fighting.e: From Middle English feghtyng, fyȝtynge, fightand, feghtand, feghtande, feightand, feȝtand, viȝtinde, feihtende, from Old English feohtende, from Proto-Germanic *fehtandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *fehtaną (“to comb, struggle, contend with”), equivalent to fight + -ing.
fighting.g: Engaged in war or other conflict.

figure.e: From Middle English figure, borrowed from Old French figure, from Latin figūra (“form, shape, form of a word, a figure of speech, Late Latin a sketch, drawing”), from fingō (“to form, shape, mold, fashion”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeyǵʰ- (“to mold, shape, form, knead”).
figure.g: A drawing or diagram conveying information.

figurehead.g: A carved figure on the prow of a sailing ship.

file.e: From Old French fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
file.g: A collection of papers collated and archived together.

file.e: From Middle English file, fyle, from Old English fēl, fēol (“file”), from earlier fīil, from Proto-Germanic *finhlō, *finhilō (“file, rasp”), from Proto-Indo-European *peyḱ- (“to adorn, form”).
file.g: A tool consisting of a strip or rod of hardened and coarse metal, used for removing sharp edges, shaping, and cutting, especially through me

filigree.e: From French filigrane, from Italian filigrana, from Latin fīlum (“thread”) + grānum (“grain”).
filigree.g: A delicate and intricate ornamentation made from platinum, gold or silver (or sometimes other metal) twisted wire.

fill.e: From Middle English fillen, fullen, from Old English fyllan (“to fill, fill up, replenish, satisfy; complete, fulfill”), from Proto-West Germanic *fullijan, from Proto-Germanic *fullijaną (“to make full, fill”), from *fullaz (“full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).
From Middle English fille, vülle, fülle, from Old English fyllu, from Proto-West Germanic *fullī, from Proto-Germanic *fullį̄ (“fullness”).
fill.g: A sufficient or more than sufficient amount.

fillet.e: From Middle English filet, vylette, felet, filette, flette, from Old French filet, diminutive of fil (“thread”), from Latin fīlum (“thread”).
fillet.g: A headband; a ribbon or other band used to tie the hair up, or keep a headdress in place, or for decoration.

filth.e: From Middle English filth, from Old English fȳlþu, from Proto-West Germanic *fūliþu, equivalent to foul + -th (abstract nominal suffix).
filth.g: Dirt; foul matter; that which soils or defiles.

filthy.e: From Middle English filthy, filthi, equivalent to filth + -y.

fin.e: From Middle English fin, from Old English finn, from Proto-Germanic *finnō, *finǭ (“dorsal fin”) (compare Dutch vin, German Finne, Swedish finne, fena), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pīn- (“backbone, dorsal fin”) (compare Old Irish ind (“end, point”), Latin pinna (“feather, wing, fin”), Tocharian A spin (“hook”).
fin.g: One of the appendages of a fish, used to propel itself and to manoeuvre/maneuver.

final.e: From Middle English final, fynal, fynall, from Old French final, from Latin fīnālis (“of or relating to the end or to boundaries”), from fīnis (“end”); see fine. Replaced native English endly (“final”).
final.g: A final examination; a test or examination given at the end of a term or class; the test that concludes a class.

finally.e: From Middle English finally, fynaly, fynally, fynaliche, fynalliche, equivalent to final + -ly.
finally.g: At the end or conclusion; ultimately.

find.e: From Middle English fynden, from Old English findan, from Proto-West Germanic *finþan, from Proto-Germanic *finþaną, a secondary verb from Proto-Indo-European *pent- (“to go, pass; path bridge”). For the meaning development compare Proto-Slavic *najьti > Russian найти́ (najtí), akin to Proto-Slavic *jьti > идти́ (idtí).

finding.e: From Middle English fyndyng, Old English findincge; equivalent to find + -ing.
finding.g: A result of research or an investigation.

fine.e: From Middle English fin, fyn, from Old French fin (“fine, minute, exact”), of obscure origin, but probably derived from Latin fīnīre (“to finish”) or fīnis (“boundary, limit, end”), with an abstract sense of fine or thin also arising in many Romance languages (compare Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish fino).
From Middle English fyn, fyne, from Old French fin, from Medieval Latin fīnis (“a payment in settlement or tax”).
fine.g: A fee levied as punishment for breaking the law.

finely.e: From Middle English finely, fynely, fynly, fineliche, finliche, fynliche, equivalent to fine + -ly.
finely.g: So as to produce a fine texture; into small, thin, or delicate pieces.

finger.e: From Middle English fynger, finger, from Old English finger (“finger”), from Proto-West Germanic *fingr, from Proto-Germanic *fingraz (“finger”), from Proto-Indo-European *penkʷrós, from *pénkʷe (“five”).
finger.g: A slender jointed extremity of the human hand, (often) exclusive of the thumb, and the corresponding part, irrespective of including a thumb

finish.e: From Middle English finishen, finisshen, finischen, from Old French finiss-, stem of some of the conjugated forms of finir, from Latin fīnīre, from fīnis (“end, limit, border, boundary”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to stick, set up”) or from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeyd- (“to split”).
finish.g: An end; the end of anything.

fir.e: From Middle English firre, from Old English fyrh, furh, as in furhwudu (“pinewood”), from Proto-West Germanic *furhu, from Proto-Germanic *furhō, *furhijǭ, from Proto-Indo-European *pŕ̥kʷeh₂, from *pérkʷus (“oak”). Possibly conflated during Middle English with Old Norse fýri (as in fýriskógr (“pine-wood”).
fir.g: A conifer of the genus Abies.

fire.e: From Middle English fyr, from Old English fȳr (“fire”), from Proto-West Germanic *fuir, from *fuïr, a regularised form of Proto-Germanic *fōr (“fire”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *péh₂wr̥.
fire.g: A (usually self-sustaining) chemical reaction involving the bonding of oxygen with carbon or other fuel, with the production of heat and the

fire.e: From Middle English firen, fyren, furen, from Old English fȳrian (“to make a fire”), from the noun (see above).
fire.g: To set (something, often a building) on fire.

firebrand.e: From Middle English fyr-brand, furbrond, equivalent to fire + brand.
firebrand.g: A torch or other burning stick with a flame at one end.

firelight.e: From Middle English fire liȝt, fyre lyghte, from Old English fȳrlēoht, equivalent to fire + light.
firelight.g: The light of a fire, such as from a campfire or fireplace.

firepan.g: A pan for holding or conveying fire, especially (firearms) the receptacle for the priming of a gun.

firepot.g: A pot used to hold or carry fire.

firewood.e: From Middle English ferwode, fyrewoode, equivalent to fire + wood.
firewood.g: Wood intended to be burned, typically for heat.

firkin.e: From Middle Dutch *vierdekijn, diminutive of vierde (“fourth”), from vier (“four”); equivalent to fourth + -kin.
firkin.g: A varying measure of capacity, usually being a quarter of a barrel; specifically, a measure equal to nine imperial gallons.

firm.e: From Italian firma (“signature”), from firmare (“to sign”), from Latin firmāre (“to make firm, to confirm (by signature)”), from firmus (“firm, stable”). The contemporary sense developed in the 18th century simultaneously with German Firma (“business, name of business”).
firm.g: A business partnership; the name under which it trades.

firm.e: From Middle English ferme, borrowed from Old French ferme, from Medieval Latin ferma. From Middle English ferme, from Old French ferme, from Latin firmus (“strong, steady”).

firmament.e: From Middle English firmament, furmament (“heaven; sky”), from Old French firmament (“firmament”), or from its etymon Latin firmāmentum (“support; sky”), from firmāre (“to strengthen”) + -mentum (suffix indicating an instrument or medium, or the result of an action). Firmāre is the present active infinitive of firmō (“to make firm, strengthen”).
firmament.g: The vault of the heavens, where the clouds, sun, moon, and stars can be seen; the heavens, the sky.

firmly.e: From Middle English fermely; equivalent to firm + -ly.
firmly.g: In a firm or definite or strong manner.

first.e: From Middle English first, furst, ferst, fyrst, from Old English fyrest, from Proto-West Germanic *furist, from Proto-Germanic *furistaz (“first, foremost”), superlative of Proto-Germanic *furai, *furi (“before”), from Proto-Indo-European *preh₂- (“before”), from *per- (“before; first”), equivalent to fore + -est.
first.g: Preceding all others of a series or kind; the ordinal of one; earliest.

first.e: From Middle English first, furst, fyrst, from Old English fyrst, fierst, first (“period, space of time, time, respite, truce”), from Proto-Germanic *frestaz, *fristiz, *frestą (“date, appointed time”), from Proto-Indo-European *pres-, *per- (“forward, forth, over, beyond”).

firstborn.e: From Middle English first borne. By surface analysis, first (adverb) + born.
firstborn.g: The first child to be born to a parent or family.

firstfruit.e: From Middle English firste fruyt, equivalent to first + fruit.
firstfruit.g: An offering of the first of the harvest; firstfruits.

firstling.g: The first produce or result, notably firstborn offspring.

firstripe.g: Of fruit, the earliest to ripen; the freshest.

fish.e: From Middle English fisch, from Old English fisċ (“fish”), from Proto-West Germanic *fisk, from Proto-Germanic *fiskaz (“fish”), from Proto-Indo-European *piskós (“fish”).
fish.g: A typically cold-blooded vertebrate animal that lives in water, moving with the help of fins and breathing with gills; any vertebrate that i
A counter, used in various games.

fisher.e: From Middle English fischer, fischare, from Old English fisċere (“fisher”), from Proto-Germanic *fiskārijaz (“fisher”), equivalent to fish + -er.
fisher.g: A person who catches fish, especially for a living or for sport; a person engaging in the pastime of fishing.

fisher.e: From French fichet (“polecat pelt”), probably from Dutch visse (“nasty”); modified by folk etymology to resemble Etymology 1.
fisher.g: A North American marten-like mammal (Pekania pennanti), that has thick brown fur.

fishhook.e: From Middle English fisch-hook, from Old English *fischōc (“fishhook”), equivalent to fish + hook.
fishhook.g: A barbed hook, usually metal, used for fishing.

fishpool.e: From Middle English fischpol, from Old English fisċpōl (“fishpond”), equivalent to fish + pool.
fishpool.g: A pool of water containing fish; fishpond.

fist.e: From Middle English fist, from Old English fȳst (“fist”), from Proto-West Germanic *fūsti (“fist”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Indo-European *pewǵ- (“to punch; to prick, stab”).
fist.g: A hand with the fingers clenched or curled inward.

fist.e: From Middle English fisten, fiesten, from Old English *fistan ("to break wind gently"; supported by Old English fisting (“breaking wind”)), from Proto-Germanic *fistaz (“breaking wind, fart”), from Proto-Germanic *fīsaną (“to break or discharge wind, fart”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)peys- (“to blow, breathe”).

fit.e: Formed from fight on the model of bite:bit and light:lit.

fitch.e: Shortening of fitchew, or directly borrowed from its antecedent, Middle Dutch vitsche (“polecat”).
fitch.g: A polecat, such as the European polecat (Mustela putorius), the striped polecat, steppe polecat, or black-footed polecat of America.

fitch.e: From fitch due to the similarity to the striped or mottled pattern of polecat fur.
fitch.g: A kind of twisted open weave in wickerwork.

fitting.e: From fit (“to conform to in shape or size; to be suitable for”, verb) + -ing (suffix forming present participles of verbs, and gerunds and nouns denoting the act of doing something or the embodiment of an action).

five.e: From Middle English fyf, fyve, from Old English fīf (“five”), from Proto-West Germanic *fimf (“five”), from Proto-Germanic *fimf (“five”), from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. The nasal *m in Proto-Germanic *fimf was lost through a sound change known as the Ingvaeonic nasal spirant law.
five.g: A numerical value equal to 5; the number following four and preceding six.

fix.e: From Middle English fixen, borrowed from Old French *fixer (attested only as ficher, fichier; > English fitch), from fix (“fastened; fixed”), from Latin fīxus (“immovable; steady; stable; fixed”), from fīgō (“to drive in; stick; fasten”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰeygʷ- (“to jab; stick; set”).
fix.g: To pierce; now generally replaced by transfix.
